title: Double-Wide Image of Pickering's Triangle
caption: Pickering's Triangle in the Cygnus Loop, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
credit: T.A. Rector/University of Alaska Anchorage, H. Schweiker/WIYN and NOIRLab/NSF/AURA

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: This wide-field view shows Pickering's Triangle, part of the Cygnus Loop supernova remnant in the constellation Cygnus, the Swan. The same remnant includes the well-known Veil Nebula.

A supernova remnant is the expanding debris of a star that exploded, sweeping up and heating the gas around it until it glows. Astronomers estimate that the explosion behind this one happened somewhere between 5,000 and 10,000 years ago. Its whole shell now stretches across more than six full Moons on the sky.

To capture it, Travis Rector and Heidi Schweiker combined two full pointings of the 64-megapixel NOAO Mosaic-1 camera, which sits on the historic Mayall 4-meter telescope, an NSF facility at Kitt Peak National Observatory. The result is a double-wide image that shows a larger slice of the remnant.
scale: Pickering's Triangle is about 1,500 light-years from Earth, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: The Mosaic-1 camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used narrowband filters that isolate light from oxygen, sulfur and hydrogen gas. The source does not say which color each filter was assigned.
filters: 502 nm · Optical Olll (NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope Mosaic I)
673 nm · Optical Sll (NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope Mosaic I)
657 nm · Optical Ha (NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope Mosaic I)
understand.eye: The remnant is too faint to see by eye. Narrow filters and long exposures bring out its glowing gas.
